analogy.p: Think of an architect's drawings of a house: one sheet shows the roof from above (the plan), another shows the front of the house as if you were standing in front of it (the front elevation), and another shows the side. No single sheet shows everything, but together they tell the builder exactly what to build. Plans and elevations work the same way: each view is flat, and you combine all three to understand the 3D solid. The analogy breaks down because real architects also draw cross-sections and show hidden details with special lines, while GCSE usually asks for only the visible outline and edges.

bullets: A **plan** is the view looking **down from above**; a **front elevation** is the view from the **front**; a **side elevation** is the view from the **side** (the question's arrow tells you which side).
You must **draw** these views from a 3D diagram or from a description, using a ruler and the grid.
You must **interpret** given views: identify the solid, count cubes, find lengths, areas and volumes.
Solids you may meet include **cuboids, prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, spheres and hemispheres**, plus **composite solids** such as cube stacks and houses.
Plans and elevations are **2D views of 3D shapes**, so lengths must be consistent between the views.
The views are drawn **to scale** when on a grid; each square usually represents 1 cm.
Edexcel questions typically give a diagram with an **arrow marked F or 'front'** to show the direction from which the front elevation is taken.
core.p: Edexcel 1MA1 (Geometry and measures, G13) asks you to **construct and interpret plans and elevations of 3D shapes**. A **plan** is the view of a solid from **above**; an **elevation** is a view from the **side or the front**, looking straight at it. You must be able to draw these views accurately (often on a centimetre grid) and to work backwards from the views to describe or sketch the solid. The topic is worth about 2 to 4 marks, shows up on all three papers, and is often combined with volume, surface area or Pythagoras. Seeing a solid as a set of flat 2D pictures is also a key skill for nets and isometric drawing.

bullets: **Plan:** look down from above; it shows the **footprint and the top** of the solid.
**Front elevation:** look horizontally at the face the arrow marks as the front.
**Side elevation:** look horizontally from the side given; from the **right**, the front of the solid appears on the **left** of your drawing.
In a standard layout the **plan is drawn above the front elevation**, and the **side elevation to the side**, so widths line up vertically and heights line up horizontally.
In a **plan**, the front of the solid is at the **bottom** of the page.
All views are **straight-on**: you do not see slanting perspective, only true lengths on the faces facing you.
Read the question carefully: 'from the direction of the arrow' overrides assumptions about left and right.
core.h: The three views and where you look from
core.p: Imagine standing in front of a solid. The **front elevation** is the shape you see looking straight at the front face. The **side elevation** is what you see after walking to the side (usually the right, if the question says 'side elevation from the direction of the arrow') and looking straight at it. The **plan** is the view from directly **above**, as a bird would see it. Each view is a flat **silhouette with internal lines** where edges and faces meet. Before drawing, work out which direction you are looking from and what the outline will be, because many marks are lost by drawing the right shape from the wrong direction.

bullets: Draw **solid lines** for every visible edge, including lines inside the outline where faces meet.
Do **not** draw lines between faces that are **flush** (in the same plane): there is no edge to see.
Use the **grid squares** and a **ruler**; each square usually represents 1 cm.

Check consistency: **width** in the plan equals **width** in the front elevation; **height** in the front elevation equals **height** in the side elevation; **depth** in the plan equals **width** in the side elevation.
Curved surfaces (cylinders, cones, spheres) give **curves in the plan** but may give straight lines in elevations.
Hidden edges, if requested, are **dashed**; otherwise leave them out.
Label dimensions only if asked; keep drawings clean and the outline closed.
core.p: Draw **exactly what you can see** looking straight at the solid. Every **visible edge** is a solid line, including edges **inside** the outline where two faces meet at different angles or at different heights. Two faces that lie in the **same flat plane** (for example two squares of the same height side by side) do **not** have an edge drawn between them, because no edge is visible. Use a **sharp pencil and ruler**, work on the given grid, and check that heights and widths match between views. Hidden edges are usually not drawn at GCSE unless the question asks for them; if you are asked, show them as **dashed lines**.

bullets: **Cuboid:** rectangle in all three views, with sizes (width x depth), (width x height) and (depth x height).
**Triangular prism** (triangle at the front): front = **triangle**, side = **rectangle**, plan = **rectangle with a line along the ridge**.
Triangular prism lying on a rectangular face with triangle at the side: the side view is the triangle and the front is a rectangle.
A **cylinder** standing upright: plan = **circle**, front and side = **rectangles**.

A **cylinder lying on its curved surface**: plan = **rectangle**; if its axis points towards you the front is a **circle** and the side a rectangle, otherwise the front is a rectangle and the side a circle.
The **cross-section** of a prism is the shape you see at the end; the **length** is the third dimension.
Check the **ridge line** of a roof or wedge: in plan it is a line, in the elevation across the ridge it is a vertex (peak).
core.h: Plans and elevations of prisms and cuboids
core.p: A **cuboid** has a rectangle for every view: the plan is a rectangle (length by width), the front elevation is a rectangle (width by height) and the side elevation is a rectangle (depth by height). A **prism** has a constant cross-section, so one view shows the **cross-section** (usually the end viewed from the front or side) and the other views show **rectangles**. For a **triangular prism** lying with its triangular face to the front, the front elevation is the **triangle**, the side elevation is a **rectangle**, and the plan is a **rectangle with a line down the middle** for the ridge (the edge where the two sloping faces meet). That middle line is a real edge seen from above, so it must be drawn.

bullets: **Square-based pyramid:** plan = square with both diagonals; front and side = isosceles triangles.
**Cone:** plan = circle (often with a dot for the apex); front and side = isosceles triangles.
**Sphere:** circle in every view (plan, front, side).
**Hemisphere** (flat face down): plan = circle; elevations = semicircles.
**Cylinder (upright):** plan = circle; elevations = rectangles.
**Triangular-based pyramid:** plan = triangle with lines from its corners to a central point where the apex sits.
**Frustum of a cone** (a cone with the top cut off): plan = two concentric circles; elevation = trapezium.
Because two different solids can share a view, always use **all three views** to decide what the solid is.
core.p: Solids that come to a point or are curved have recognisable views. A **square-based pyramid** has a **square with diagonals** as its plan (the diagonals are the edges from the apex to the four corners, seen from above), and **triangles** as its front and side elevations. A **cone** has a **circle with a dot at the centre** as its plan (the dot is the apex) and **triangles** as its elevations. A **sphere** looks like a **circle** from every direction. A **hemisphere** with its flat face down has a **circle** as its plan and a **semicircle** as its elevations. A cone and a pyramid both give triangular elevations, so the plan is what tells you which solid you have.

bullets: **Plan numbers** give the height of the stack in each position; **sum them for the total number of cubes**.
**Front elevation:** for each column left to right, draw the **maximum** height of stacks in that column (looking from front to back).
**Side elevation from the right:** for each row from **front to back** (left to right on the page), draw the **maximum** height in that row.
Draw the **grid lines** between squares in the elevation only if the question's style does; otherwise outline the shape and show edges as asked (cube stacks on a grid usually show each square).
Hidden cubes behind taller stacks **do not appear** in an elevation.
To find the **volume** of a cube stack with 1 cm cubes, add the numbers: volume in **cm cubed** equals the number of cubes.
To find the **surface area**, count the visible faces from all six directions (top and bottom from plan, four sides from the elevations), allowing for hidden faces inside.
If asked for the **maximum or minimum number of cubes** that fit given views, use the views to set minimum heights and maximum possible fillers.
core.p: Many exam questions use solids built from **cubes** or from a cuboid with a roof. For a stack of cubes, the **plan** shows the footprint and often the **number of cubes in each position**. To draw an elevation you look along a line of sight and draw, for each column of the view, the **tallest stack** in that direction, because taller stacks hide shorter ones. The side elevation viewed from the right shows the **front of the solid on the left**. Counting all the cubes means **adding the numbers in the plan**. For example, a plan with rows 3 / 2, 2 / 1, 1, 2 has 3 + 4 + 4 = 11 cubes, a front elevation of heights 3, 2, 2 and a side elevation (from the right) of heights 2, 2, 3.

bullets: **Front elevation (gable end):** a house shape: rectangle plus triangle.
**Side elevation:** a **rectangle** with a **horizontal line at the eaves** (where the wall meets the roof).
**Plan:** a **rectangle** with the **ridge line** along the middle (if the roof overhangs, extra lines show the overhang).
If the roof ridge runs across the front instead, the views swap: the front becomes the rectangle with a line and the side becomes the house shape.
Total height = **wall height + roof rise**; use this to check the elevations.
Where two parts meet at the **same height**, no line is drawn between them; where heights differ, **draw the line**.
This kind of question often asks you to draw one elevation on the grid and then **find the volume** of the shed.
core.h: Combined solids: houses, sheds and roofs
core.p: A **shed or house** is a cuboid (walls) topped with a triangular prism (roof). The **front elevation** shows a **pentagon** (a rectangle with a triangle on top, 'a house shape') when the gable end faces the front. The **side elevation** shows a **rectangle** whose height is the wall height plus the roof rise, with a **horizontal line** at the height where the wall meets the sloping roof (the eaves), because that is a real edge you can see. The **plan** is a **rectangle with the ridge line** drawn down the middle. Every line you draw must be an edge of the solid or an outline you can see.

bullets: **Width:** plan = front elevation.
**Height:** front elevation = side elevation.
**Depth:** plan = side elevation width.
Use these links to **find missing dimensions** and to **check** your drawn views.
If a **scale** is given (for example 1 square = 2 cm), multiply the grid length to get the real length.
To find the **slant height** or an unknown length in an elevation of a cone or pyramid, use **Pythagoras' theorem** on the right-angled triangle in the elevation.
For angle of slope, use **trigonometry** on the same triangle.
core.h: Reading dimensions and lining up the views
core.p: The three views of the same solid must agree on the dimensions they share. **Width** is the same in the plan and the front elevation, **height** is the same in the front elevation and the side elevation, and **depth (length)** is the same in the plan and the side elevation. That gives you **three checks** and lets you find missing lengths: if the plan shows a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle and the front elevation has the same width 6 cm, then the side elevation must have width equal to the depth 4 cm of the plan. On a grid, count squares carefully and convert if a scale is given.

bullets: **Plan circle + front triangle + side triangle:** **cone**.
**Plan square with diagonals + triangular elevations:** **square-based pyramid**.
**Plan circle + two rectangles:** **cylinder**.
**Circle in all three views:** **sphere**.
**Plan rectangle with a middle line + triangle + rectangle:** **triangular prism**.
**Three rectangles:** **cuboid** (three squares: cube).
For cube stacks, the plan gives positions, the elevations give maximum heights, and the **minimum** and **maximum** totals come from the views.
After deciding, **sketch the solid** and check that each of its views matches the given ones.
core.h: Working backwards: identifying a solid from its views
core.p: Some questions give the three views and ask you to name or sketch the solid. Treat each view as a clue: a **circle plan with triangles in the elevations** is a **cone**, a **square plan with diagonals and triangular elevations** is a **square-based pyramid**, **rectangles in all three views** means a **cuboid** (or a cube if the dimensions are equal), and **circle, rectangle, rectangle** is an upright **cylinder**. A **rectangle plan with a ridge line, a triangle for one elevation and a rectangle for the other** is a **triangular prism**. Use all three views because one view alone is never enough: a circle plan could be a cone, cylinder, sphere or hemisphere.

bullets: **Volume of a prism = cross-sectional area x length.** For a triangular prism: (1/2 x base x height) x length.
**Cuboid volume = length x width x height.**
**Cone volume = (1/3) x pi x r squared x h**, and **sphere volume = (4/3) x pi x r cubed** (both given on the Edexcel formulae page).
**Surface area** = total area of all faces; use plan and elevations to find the face shapes.

For a **cone or pyramid**, find the slant height with **Pythagoras**: slant height squared = height squared + (half base)^2 for the right-angled triangle in the elevation (for a cone, base radius instead of half the base).
Always include **units**: cm^2 for area and cm^3 for volume.
Combine with **scale factors** if two solids are similar.
core.h: Using views to find area and volume
core.p: Plans and elevations are a bridge to measures. The **cross-section** of a prism is the shape in one elevation, so **volume of a prism = area of cross-section x length**. The **footprint area** from the plan can give the area of the base. Each face of a polyhedron appears as a true shape in some view, which lets you work out **surface area** by adding the areas of all faces. In a cone or pyramid, the **vertical height** is seen in an elevation, and the right-angled triangle in the elevation links height, half the base and **slant height**. Check each calculation carefully and give units: **cm squared for area, cm cubed for volume**.

bullets: **Isometric paper:** vertical lines stay vertical; other edges are drawn at **30 degrees** to the horizontal.
A **net** unfolds a solid into a flat shape; for a prism it is a **strip of rectangles** plus **two end faces**.
Counting faces in the views helps check a net (a cuboid has 6 faces, a triangular prism 5).
A cube stack can be drawn from its plan with numbers and its elevations.
If you must **sketch** a solid from views, start with the plan and add heights from the elevations.
These skills link to **surface area**: the areas of the faces in the net equal the surface area.
core.h: Isometric drawings, nets and the link to 3D
core.p: Plans and elevations are **orthogonal views**; they connect to other ways of drawing solids. An **isometric drawing** shows all three faces in one picture on isometric (triangular dotted) paper, with vertical edges drawn vertically and the other edges at 30 degrees to the horizontal. A **net** is a flat pattern that folds into a solid, and its faces match the shapes you see in the views. Being able to move between views, an isometric picture and a net helps you spot errors: each face in the net must match a face seen in some elevation or plan.

bullets: Read the **arrow direction** and decide the orientation before drawing.
Count grid squares carefully; **lengths must be exact** on the grid (usually within a small tolerance).
Include **internal lines** where faces meet at different heights; missing them often loses a mark.
Do not draw **extra lines** between flush faces.
For 'name the solid' questions, give the **name** and a reason that uses the views.
Show full working for volume or area in context and **include units**.
If a sketch is required, make it **neat and labelled**; if drawing is required, use a ruler.
Check the final picture by **comparing widths and heights** between the views.
core.h: Exam skills, mark allocation and typical question types
core.p: Typical Edexcel questions show a solid on a grid (often a cube stack, prism or combined shape) and say 'On the centimetre grid, draw the front elevation / side elevation / plan from the direction of the arrow'. A 2 or 3 mark question usually awards **1 mark for the correct outline and 1 or 2 marks for correct internal lines or exact dimensions**. Questions about identifying a solid usually give **1 mark for naming** and **1 mark for a reason**. Work slowly: examiners check line lengths on the grid exactly, so every square matters. Use a ruler and make sure the **outline is closed**.

bullets: **Volume and surface area** of prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres and pyramids.
**Pythagoras' theorem** and **trigonometry** in right-angled triangles seen in the elevations.
**Scale drawing:** convert grid length to real length.
**Maps and bearings:** a plan view is like a map seen from above.
**Similar solids:** length scale factor k, area k^2, volume k^3.
**Nets and isometric drawings** use the same faces and edges.
core.p: Plans and elevations connect to many parts of the course. They support **volume and surface area** (prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres, pyramids), **Pythagoras and trigonometry** (using the right-angled triangle in an elevation to find slant heights and angles), **scale drawings and ratio** (scale on the grid), **bearings** (a plan view is like a map) and **similar shapes** (scale factors for lengths, areas and volumes). At Higher tier, combined solids often need more than one formula, and you may be asked to find the **angle between a line and a plane** using the elevation.

exam: The command words are **draw**, **sketch**, **describe** and **name**; use a ruler for **draw** and be neat for **sketch**.
Typical marks: **2 to 3 marks** for drawing a view (outline plus internal lines); each correct view is usually one mark.
Always check the **direction of the arrow** to decide what the front elevation is.
For **cube stacks**, draw the tallest stack for each column or row; do not add hidden cubes.
**Plan numbers** summed give the total number of cubes; show the addition for the method mark.
For **'name the solid'** give the name and a reason from the views, e.g. 'the plan is a circle and the elevations are triangles, so it is a cone'.
For **volume of a prism**, state **area of cross-section x length** and show the cross-section area calculation.
Give **units**: cm^2 for area and cm^3 for volume; use the formulae page for cone and sphere.
Use **Pythagoras** on the elevation to find a slant height; draw the right-angled triangle to help.
On a grid, **count squares carefully** and use a ruler; examiners check lengths exactly.
If a scale is given, convert before drawing or after measuring.
Use the figure habit: lightly project dashed lines from one view to the next so the widths and heights line up exactly on the grid.

mistakes.r: Plan is from above; elevations are looking horizontally at the front or the side.
mistakes.w: Drawing the plan from the front or the elevation from above.

mistakes.r: Every visible edge must be drawn, including edges inside the outline.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the line inside the outline where two faces of different heights meet.

mistakes.r: No edge is visible between flush faces, so no line should be drawn.
mistakes.w: Drawing a line between two flush faces (same height, same plane).

mistakes.r: From the right, the front of the solid is on the left of your drawing; follow the arrow in the question.
mistakes.w: Mixing up left and right on the side elevation.

mistakes.r: Only the tallest stack in each line of sight appears; hidden parts are not shown (unless dashed lines are requested).
mistakes.w: Including hidden cubes or hidden edges in the elevation of a cube stack.

mistakes.r: The plan of a cone is a circle (with a dot at the apex); the triangle is the elevation.
mistakes.w: Giving the plan of a cone as just a triangle.

mistakes.r: Width, height and depth must agree between the plan and elevations; check each against the others.
Volume is in cubed units, for example cm cubed.
mistakes.w: Giving the volume of a cube stack without units, or using the wrong units.

mistakes.r: Check the three views agree: width in plan = front, height in front = side, depth in plan = side.
mistakes.w: Drawing views whose shared dimensions do not match.

summary: The specification asks you to construct and interpret the plan (view from above) and the front and side elevations of 3D shapes, including prisms, pyramids, cones and combined solids. It matters because exam questions give marks for exact line drawing and consistent views, and they link to volume, surface area and Pythagoras.

terms.d: The view of a 3D shape looking down from directly above.
The view of a 3D shape looking horizontally at its front face.
The view of a 3D shape looking horizontally at one of its sides.
A view of a 3D shape from the front or the side, drawn as a 2D picture.
The shape you see when you cut straight through a solid; for a prism it is the same all along its length.
A solid with the same cross-section all along its length.
A solid with six rectangular faces.
A solid with a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at a point (the apex).
The top point of a cone or pyramid.
A line where two faces of a solid meet.
A flat surface of a solid.
A corner where edges meet (plural: vertices).
The top edge of a roof where two sloping faces meet.
An edge that cannot be seen from the viewing direction; shown with dashed lines when required.
A 3D drawing on triangular dotted paper with vertical lines vertical and other lines at 30 degrees.
A flat shape that folds up to make a solid.
The length along the sloping face of a cone or pyramid from the base edge to the apex.
The shape the base of a solid makes on the ground, seen in the plan.
The horizontal edge where the wall of a house or shed meets the sloping roof; it shows as a line across the side elevation.
The triangular end wall of a pitched roof; when it faces the front, the front elevation is a house shape.

worked.ans: (a) Front elevation with columns of height 3, 2, 2 squares. (b) Volume = 11 cm cubed.
worked.q: (3 marks) A solid is made from 1 cm cubes. The plan shows the number of cubes in each position. Back row: 3 (left position only). Middle row: 2, 2. Front row: 1, 1, 2. (a) Draw the front elevation. (b) Work out the volume of the solid.
steps: Front elevation looks from the front, so for each column take the tallest stack: column 1 has stacks 3, 2, 1 so the tallest is 3; column 2 has 0, 2, 1 so the tallest is 2; column 3 has 0, 0, 2 so the tallest is 2.
Draw bars of heights 3, 2, 2 squares left to right.
Volume = number of cubes: add the plan numbers: 3 + (2 + 2) + (1 + 1 + 2) = 3 + 4 + 4 = 11.
Each cube has volume 1 cm cubed, so the volume is 11 cm cubed.

worked.ans: Plan: 4 cm by 6 cm rectangle with a middle line. Front: triangle (base 4, height 3). Side: 6 cm by 3 cm rectangle. Volume = 36 cm cubed.
worked.q: (3 marks) A triangular prism has an isosceles triangle cross-section with base 4 cm and height 3 cm, and the prism is 6 cm long. It rests on a rectangular face with the triangle facing the front. Describe the plan, front elevation and side elevation, and find the volume.
steps: Front elevation is the triangle: base 4 cm, height 3 cm.
Side elevation is a rectangle 6 cm long and 3 cm high (the ridge is at height 3 cm).
Plan is a rectangle 4 cm by 6 cm with a line along the middle (2 cm from each long side) for the ridge.
Cross-section area = 1/2 x 4 x 3 = 6 cm squared.
Volume = cross-section area x length = 6 x 6 = 36 cm cubed.

worked.ans: A cone; volume = 12 pi = 37.7 cm cubed (3 s.f.).
worked.q: (3 marks) The plan of a solid is a circle of diameter 6 cm with a dot at its centre. The front elevation is an isosceles triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm. Name the solid and work out its volume. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps: A circle plan with a dot and a triangular elevation is a cone.
Radius = 6 / 2 = 3 cm and height h = 4 cm.
Volume of a cone = (1/3) x pi x r squared x h = (1/3) x pi x 9 x 4.
